newsitem.title: USA: Senators raise doubts on CIA nominee Lake.
newsitem.headline: Senators raise doubts on CIA nominee Lake.

text.p: Republicans on the Senate Intelligence Committee said on Sunday they were troubled by President Bill Clinton's nomination of Anthony Lake to head the CIA and declined to predict he would be confirmed.

Sen. Richard Shelby, the panel's incoming chairman, denied a suggestion that Republicans had chosen Lake, currently the White House national security adviser, to be their "whipping boy" among Clinton's second-term Cabinet nominees.

"Any nominee, including Mr. Lake, should be one with the highest integrity above everything. And some past conduct troubles me, as it troubles a lot of other people in the Senate," Shelby said on the ABC programme "This Week."

The Alabama Republican was referring to Lake's role in keeping secret a 1994 White House decision that the United States would not object when Croatia allowed Iranian arms to be shipped through its territory to Bosnia.
Lake also faces questions about possible conflicts of interest because he failed to take timely action on orders to sell off his personal holdings in energy stocks.
Shelby said the hearings would be "searching and thorough" and the committee would "scrutinize" both issues. He added, "It's too early to predict what will happen."
Sen. Arlen Specter of Pennsylvania, the outgoing Republican Intelligence Committee chairman, said in a separate interview on CNN's "Late Edition" that Lake's confirmation was "up in the air."

Clinton has defended Lake, saying nothing disqualified him from serving as CIA director. White House Chief of Staff Leon Panetta said on Sunday that Lake had made "a simple oversight" in the stocks matter and conceded it probably would have been better to work more closely with Congress on the arms issue.
"I think he's an excellent candidate and I think he's going to be confirmed," Panetta said on NBC's "Meet the Press."
Lake has told lawmakers in telephone calls during the past week that he made a mistake in not informing Congress of the Bosnian arms decision.
Current CIA Director John Deutch on Sunday agreed that it was an error of judgment, saying someone in the administration should have informed Congress of the arms transfer.
"I think with hindsight, most of the leadership in the administration believes that as well. And I believe Tony Lake believes it," he said in an interview on ABC's "This Week."
The Republicans appeared unmollified by Lake's admission, and Shelby said it did not close the book on the issue because the administration's policy had been "duplicitous" from the beginning.
"I think it's too early to say what we will do with his nomination. But I think we've got to be fair and searching and we've got to scrutinise this," he added.
Specter said, "It is a serious matter .... it is important that the CIA be open with Congress."
Shelby hinted at the possibility of the White House withdrawing Lake's nomination sometime in the future as Clinton did with several of his first-term nominees when controversies arose.
However Shelby said he was not calling on the president to do so "at this time."
"But we've all seen a lot of nominations never be sent up after public scrutiny. Let's see what happens in the next several weeks on Mr. Lake," he said.
